subject: Multiplex orchestration capacity matrix & traffic profiling for private GPU pools
content:
From: kimberly_park@redwood.ai
To: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, laura_bennett@redwood.ai, dylan_brooks@redwood.ai, sara@orionhealth.com
Date: 2026-10-30T08:15:00-07:00
Subject: Multiplex orchestration capacity matrix & traffic profiling for private GPU pools

Team / Sara,

Putting this thread together to lock down the capacity targets and failover matrix for the Orion Health private deployment. The two asks for today:

1) Confirm throughput targets (QPS, sustained concurrency, tokens/sec) and recommended warm-pool sizing for the initial 3-week ramp.
2) Agree on admission control thresholds and graceful degradation behavior (model fallback, shard shedding, per-tenant queuing).

What I attached: capacity_matrix_v2.xlsx (proforma numbers and sensitivity table) and network_topology_diagram.svg (VPC peering, cross-region fabric).

Quick context: Orion expects bursty bot-generated traffic around specific ETL windows (08:00–10:00 local) and steady interactive queries during the day. Traffic is highly multimodal — short single-turn prompts (~20 tokens) and periodic long-context evaluations (~2k tokens). We need the multiplex orchestration plan to preserve tail latency SLOs for interactive queries while absorbing background batch workloads.

Initial constraints:
- Private pool: 16 x A100-like GPUs (4 pods of 4) in primary region, cold standby of 4 GPUs in secondary region.
- On-prem interconnect: 25 Gbps cross-rack; egress to customer network is metered.

Please review the sheet and reply with numbers / disagreements. If we agree, I’ll convert this into the admission-control runbook and a short canary test plan.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Sr. Product Manager, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Multiplex orchestration capacity matrix & traffic profiling for private GPU pools

Kimberly —

I ran an initial traffic profile from the sample logs Orion provided and fed it into the sensitivity tab in capacity_matrix_v2. Key takeaways and my suggested targets:

- Baseline QPS: 220 qps (mixed short+long)
- Sustained concurrent requests: 380 active requests (mix of short and medium sequences)
- Token throughput requirement (steady): ~45k tokens/sec across the pool; peak burst requirement: ~120k tokens/sec for 3–5 minute windows
- Preferred batching: dynamic batching with max micro-batch of 16 for short queries, multi-step batching for long requests (batch size 4) to avoid latency tail amplification
- Warm-pool sizing: 25% of GPUs warmed for immediate handling (4 GPUs), 50% warmed within 2 minutes (8 GPUs), full population within 10 minutes (16 GPUs)
- KV cache hit target: >= 70% for conversational flows to reduce compute footprint

Admission-control recommendations:
- Soft limit: 450 concurrent in the queue — beyond that, issue 503 with Retry-After and route non-interactive jobs to delayed batch queue.
- Hard limit: 550 concurrent — start rejecting by tenant priority.
- Graceful degradation order: 1) reduce max batch size for background jobs, 2) switch background jobs to cheaper quantized model, 3) shed lowest-priority tenants, 4) fail to 503 for interactive low-priority flows.

I populated the sensitivity matrix with cost/latency tradeoffs; see the "SLO vs cost" tab. We should pick a target 99th percentile latency SLO (suggest 600ms for short queries, 2.5s for long) and tune the admission thresholds accordingly.

— Karthik
Principal Systems Engineer

Subject: Re: Multiplex orchestration capacity matrix & traffic profiling for private GPU pools

Kimberly / all —

Thanks Karthik — the numbers look sane from infra side but we need to call out networking constraints more explicitly. Notes:

- Cross-rack bandwidth (25 Gbps) is the gating factor for KV cache sync and model shard transfers during warmup. If we do a full-pop warmup in 10 minutes we should avoid simultaneous bulk transfers — stagger pod bring-up across racks (ramp window = 10m, stagger = 90s).
- Egress to customer (Orion) is billed per GB; the sensitivity tab underestimates egress during long-context evaluation. Add a buffer of +30% egress for planning numbers.
- BGP / failover: set health-check TTL to 10s for routing to secondary region and prefer model-variant fallback locally before cross-region failover to avoid egress charges and cold-start penalties.
- Network QoS: mark interactive flows DSCP CS5 to prioritize on switches; background batch flows CS1. We'll need customer switch ACLs to accept DSCP codepoints.

Operational items for the runbook:
- Warm-pool orchestration should include a "noisy neighbor" throttling probe that nominates pods for background shedding.
- Circuit breaker: if packet loss > 0.5% for 30s, trigger regional read-only mode and shift interactive flows to local quantized model.

CC'ing Dylan to draft the runbook sections for warm-pool orchestration and BGP failover tests.

Laura Bennett
Sr. Infra PM

Thanks, team — this is very helpful. A few clarifying questions from Orion's side before we sign off: 

1) For the 99th percentile latency SLOs you suggested, what safety margin are you building for unexpected traffic spikes (e.g., a background job misfire)?
2) Can you provide a short table mapping degradation steps to customer-visible behavior (e.g., step 1 = batch throttling, minor QoS impact; step 4 = interactive 503 for non-critical tenants)? We want to surface this to our ops on-call playbooks.
3) Is cross-region failover strictly manual for the first 2 months? If automatic, what is the expected cold-start penalty to include in our SLA table?

Also — we will confirm acceptance of DSCP markers with network team but please keep the fallbacks non-disruptive to patient-facing queries.

— Sara (Ops lead, Orion Health)

From: kimberly_park@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-10-30T15:00:00-07:00
To: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, laura_bennett@redwood.ai, dylan_brooks@redwood.ai, sara@orionhealth.com
Subject: Re: Multiplex orchestration capacity matrix & traffic profiling for private GPU pools

Sara / team —

Nice questions — quick answers and concrete next steps below. I’ll also update the sheet with a "customer-visible impact" tab and a short matrix for SLA language.

1) Safety margin: we recommend a 20–30% headroom above the modeled 99th-percentile capacity for the first 90 days (we used 25% in the sensitivity sheet). This is delivered by the staggered warm-up and the 4-GPU cold standby in the secondary region.

2) Degradation mapping (short):
   - Step A (soft congestion): throttle background batches; interactive unaffected except slight increase in queueing latency (~+50–100ms).
   - Step B (moderate): reduce batch sizes for background jobs; quantized model fallback for background jobs; interactive 99th may increase to target +30%.
   - Step C (severe): tenant-based shedding — non-critical tenants receive 503; critical tenants still served potentially on quantized model with degraded quality.
   - Step D (critical/failed): region failover / read-only mode — interactive flows served from secondary with expected cold-start penalty per-request of 400–800ms depending on model weights cached state.

3) Failover mode: default is manual for first 60 days. After validation and three successful canaries we can enable semi-automatic failover with human-in-the-loop decision (auto-trigger + 5 minute approval window). Cold-start penalty: model-variant local fallback preferred (quantized) — cross-region cold-start observed in simulation ~600ms median, tail up to 1.2s depending on egress and cache hit. We will document this in SLA appendix.

Action items: 
- Karthik: capture admission thresholds in the runbook (due EOD 2026-11-02).
- Laura: network QOS and egress buffer language for SOW (due 2026-11-03).
- Dylan: draft warm-pool orchestration play steps + canary test plan (due 2026-11-04).
- Kimberly: update capacity_matrix_v2.xlsx with customer-visible impact tab + finalize matrix for review (due 2026-11-01).

If that timeline works for Orion, we’ll ship the runbook and a 2-hour canary window next week.

Thanks everyone —
Kimberly
Sr. Product Manager, Redwood Inference
